utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Our next witness is Hysni Kryeziu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I have an administrative issue to raise as the first thing of the morning. In the OTP's pre-trial brief they put forth the witnesses to be heard under 92 bis proposing that there be no cross-examination. In that brief, they stated all of the statements that fall within Rule 92 bis per witness. Since this is the end of the week and we only have one witness left, Mr. Stamp sent an e-mail yesterday with certain proposals that were accepted by Defence, and that part of it is fine. But again there's something I noticed, it is the following: Certain statements that were in the 92 bis package in the pre-trial brief are now missing from the list. And we said whatever was on the list was part of the package, and what is not does not need to be made part of the package. Everything that was contained in the pre-trial brief under 92 bis should be contained on this list as well. If you had not allowed those witnesses to be cross-examined, all of those statements would have made it in anyhow. Therefore, those statements should not be omitted as the Prosecutor is seeking to have now because they were part of the earlier package. That was my objection concerning their conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar, this is not the first time this issue has arisen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, and, Your Honours, I'm not sure exactly of the nature of the specific complaint in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The complaint is that you are not tendering some of the statements or past transcript of this witness which was put forward in the motion that the witness be a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And is that relating to Mr. Kryeziu, or is that relating to future witnesses? I'm not sure what the reference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It must be to the present witness, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Perhaps then if I could have a moment to review it. I'm not sure actually which exhibit my friend is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Djurdjic, which statement or past transcript is not now included?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I opened the pre-trial brief package relating to the next witness, Hani Hoxha, I believe, and the Milutinovic transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you identify the missing statement or transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Enough said. Not your baby, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And I thank my friend, I think that clears it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we will ask whichever of your colleagues we can expect next to look at it before we finish this witness so that we can be advised specifically about the reason, if any, for the omission of the transcript in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because normally, documents were put forward for admission under 92 bis, we've allowed that, but subject to cross-examination in the case of this coming witness; and normally, therefore, the documents you put forward would be part of the evidence once tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll move on then, Mr. Behar, and have something looked at before the witness arrives. Now, your witness is not that one, but Mr. Kryeziu.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If you wish, you can be seated straightaway, but we would ask you to read aloud the affirmation shown to you. Sorry, you can be seated straightaway, if you wish, but we would also ask you to read aloud an affirmation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Behar has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, thank you for joining us this morning. If you could please state your full name and your date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Hysni Kryeziu. And I was born on the 12th of April, 1949, in Reti village, Rahovec municipality, and I live in the ex-Dushanove village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and I understand that you are currently living in Switzerland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you gave an initial statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of May, 1999, about the events that you experienced in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand as well that you provided a very brief additional statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 19th of September, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Have you had the chance to read those statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you did make a number of corrections to your statement of the 14th of May, 1999, when you testified in the Milutinovic case; but I wanted to ask you, with the exception of those changes, are you satisfied that the information that's contained in the two statements that I've just mentioned is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender those two statements. I can indicate they are both under 65 ter number 02514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statements of the 14th of May, 1999, and the 19th of September, 2001, will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 14th of May, 1999, Your Honours, will be signed P00876; and the 19th of September, 2001 will be assigned P00877, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying at the trial of Mr. Milutinovic on the 29th and the 30th of November, 2006?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review the transcript of your testimony in that trial, or more specifically, to go through it with a language interpreter?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Does that transcript accurately reflect your evidence, and would you testify to the same facts today?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that transcript at 65 ter number 05030, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00878, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just before we move on, I can indicate, Your Honours, there was an exhibit that was referred to by the Prosecution at page 7546 of the transcript in which Mr. Kryeziu identified a number of vehicles that were used by Serb forces. I can indicate that exhibit was P01325 in Milutinovic. It's already been admitted in this case as P00318. I can now provide a brief summary of Mr. Kryeziu's evidence for the Court. Mr. Kryeziu describes activities by Serb forces in Dushanove, a neighborhood of Prizren, from spring 1998 to March 1999. He explains that the area was often surrounded by Serb police and VJ with tanks and are armoured vehicles. He also describes how in August of 1998, the Serb police commander, Milos Scekic, came to his house while collecting weapons and threatened to burn down houses in the village as he had done in other villages. Soon after, Serb police in dark blue uniforms and camouflage uniforms surrounded the village and then physically beat Mr. Kryeziu and his son. Mr. Kryeziu also describes the events of the 28th of March, 1999. At that time, large numbers of Serb police and VJ again surrounded his village and started to fire their weapons. They shouted at the residents to go to Albania, yelling things like "Kosovo belongs to Serbia, you belong to Albania."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kryeziu describes the whole village moving into a convoy. He and his family left the village with the convoy, in their car. He describes being stopped by police about 500 metres away and recognising police commander Scekic who had a stocking over his head. Police took away the family's car, jewellery, money, and documents. Mr. Kryeziu describes walking in the convoy of villagers for about 40 kilometres. He describes how the villagers were mistreated along the way, being robbed and beaten. And he describes arriving at the Albanian border check-point, recognising a Serb policeman from Dushanove called Nebojsa. He saw police taking money from the refugees, confiscating their cars, documents, and removing their vehicle registration plates. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I do have some very brief questions for you in the time we have remaining. In your statement you describe, of course, some of the events that took place on the 28th of March, 1999, and I know that you described that the village was surrounded by police and military, they were shooting and yelling at people to go to Albania and that the village then formed into a convoy. I have some questions for you about that convoy. And the first question is: Can you tell us the ethnicity of the people who were in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: They were Albanian. There were also some Roma or Ashkali as we call them. They were turned back with their families after travelling for about 2 or 3 kilometres. They were told that you don't need to go to Albania, you can go back to your homes, there were some Goranies [Realtime transcript read in error "grannies"] as well who were likewise returned. Therefore it was only us Albanians that were forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, who turned those people back?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Police. Police, the military. They were in mixed groups. We couldn't tell exactly who was who, but we saw it with your own eyes. A neighbour of ours was asked to go back, but they were also -- were also mistreated, but they were turned back. This is something I eye-witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I know that in your answer you just described two groups. The first was Roma that were turned back, and then there was a second, I'm not sure it came through. Can you explain to us what the second group was, who these people were?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, we call the Romas sometimes Egyptians, Ashkali, but usually we call them gypsies. They were the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And was there another group that you referenced? I can see in the English translation it says there were some "grannies" as well who were likewise returned. I'm just wanting to clarify who that other group who was returned was?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: They were Goranies, but they were not forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, am I correct that that's a group of non-Albanian Muslims you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's clearer. In your statement, sir, you also refer to the conditions briefly in the convoy when you were forced to walk for 40 kilometres after your car was taken away. You describe soldiers maltreating you, grabbing jewellery from women, at one point grabbing a baby and throwing it into the mud. Can you tell us who those forces were who were doing that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: They were Serb, Serbian Yugoslav police and military forces. And on the 28th of March at about 1700 hours, first there was a Lada Niva vehicle, a white one, that entered the village, and they started to shoot. We went inside the houses, and then we started to hear the shelling. We started to see tanks, armoured cars coming into the village, and heard yelling and shouting like, "you do not belong here. Kosova is not yours, go to Albania." They mentioned Thaqi and Rugova --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I'll stop you there if I can because we have that from your statement already, and I know you've been quite clear in describing that. I just have a couple of other very specific questions, and I know I don't have much time remaining. I wanted to ask you, sir, as you were proceeding again in this convoy when you were on foot, did you observe these Serb forces that you saw using any vehicles as you proceeded in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. There were vehicles but, as I said earlier, we were forced to form a convoy, and we had to walk straight without daring to see on the right or on the left for about 2 kilometres up to the end of the village to the road that goes to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And after you reached that point and continued on, can you explain what the -- what, if any, the police presence was like at that time, as you continued past those two kilometres?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There was a group of policemen at the place where the road turns towards Albania, and there was -- on the left there is a road that a goes to Putnik, there were police there and cars, vehicles pass by with Albanian families. They escorted them and with automatic rifles they broke their windows, car windows, and shouted at the people intimidating them. I wanted to mention that between the Printex factory and another place, I saw, everybody saw it, that they caught a baby and threw him or her on the ground. This is all we could see because, as I said, we were very scared. They -- we put the young men and women in our middle because we were afraid they would take away them from the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And as you proceeded on foot, do you recall passing any check-points? And if so, can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. When we passed Zhur, I don't know how many kilometres it is far from the border, there was a police check-point. There were sand sacks there, many people were stopped there and taken out of the convoy. When we went to the border with Albania, I met Nebojsa, a policeman, who was my neighbour with whom I had been living for about 40 years. And he asked me in Albanian, Where is your car? I told him what had happened, how the police commander had taken it away from me, and I told him about everything that had happened, how we were robbed of our documents, of our precious possessions, jewellery, and so on. I saw that most of the people were stripped of their documents. The women were taken away their jewellery, that they were maltreated, there were many instances of maltreatment on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Those are my questions for you. And my learned friend from the Defence will have some questions for you now. Sorry, Your Honours, just before I continue, I realise with the second statement, I may have misspoken about the date. I think it was recorded as 2001 it was tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be 2004?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic. We leave the prospect before you that we might finish two witnesses today, Mr. Djurdjic. We just raise that prospect for you to keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, but I'm afraid it doesn't depend on me but on the witness and the answers I receive. As you witnessed yesterday, if a witness provides brief and accurate answers, then we move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kryeziu. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, a team member of the Defence team of the accused Mr. Djordjevic. With me is Ms. Marie O'Leary, another Defence team member. I have a few questions for you in order to clarify some details from your statements which I read. Firstly, did you know Rexhep Krasniqi in 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, if we are talking about the same person, namely my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday or the day before, did you see this neighbour of yours here in The Hague, that is to say, Rexhep Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw him on the street. I think yesterday it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore we are talking about that person that you saw yesterday. In Dusanovo, where is his house located?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It is in the transit road, we call it. From my house as the crow flies, it is about 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand correctly, his house is along the main road, the road between Prizren and Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, no. It's the transit road which goes towards the villages where the German KFOR was based. It's that road, and it's about 150 metres away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is your house located?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: On the side of the transit road, and it's about 150 metres away from the Prizren-Gjakove road, main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are your house and Mr. Krasniqi's house on the same street?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 28th of March, 1999, did you see Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I didn't see him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Didn't know where my son was, let alone Rexhep, where he was. But I've seen many people being chased out of their homes from the Serb police and military, but I didn't know where my son and daughter was, let alone Rexhep.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what was or is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Shaip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was he alive in 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: My father died in 1963 in Reti village where I was born. That's in the Rahovec municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your father's occupation?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: My father was a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you move to Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: In 1963 we bought the house. In fact, in 1964 we moved with all the family to Dushanove.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who were your family members when you moved?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We were about 22 members of the family. We lived in one house. Although my father had died in 1964, my mother died too, and we buried her in the village where she was born. So we lived for a long time with her uncles and the sons of my uncles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many brothers and sisters did you have in 1964?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: With three brothers and we have one sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many of your uncles moved with you to Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I had an uncle who in fact we called father because he brought us up, and the same applied to his wife. She was our mother. And we lived in the same house with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall who you bought the plot of land from?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. He worked in the finance department of the land registry. I cannot give you any further details. I can't remember because I was young and it's about over 50 years ago, more than that that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which Serb families do you know of having lived in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Our neighbour was Slobodan Petkovic, Stanisa Petkovic, Peta Tasic, although he later moved to Prizren. We had Nebojsa. But there was some Plaskic, Estanic [phoen] who worked in hospital but later moved to Serbia. We had very good relations at the time up until the moment that the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You don't know his last name but where did he live?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I can't remember. I knew where his house was, that's on the road Prizren-Gjakove. I cannot remember his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, so next to the road Prizren-Djakovica. What about Milos Scekic, where did he live?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: He was living closer to my house, about 5 to 600 metres away, and he was near the Prizren-Gjakove Road. They had some land there and he lived in an old house. There were two brothers. His father, Slavko [Realtime transcript read in error "Slatko"] worked in the railway company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It should be "Slavko" in the transcript. Not "Slatko."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was Milos Scekic's job with the police?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Milos Scekic was a police commander, but I do not know any further details, because I wasn't working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you were a barber? You probably still are a barber?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I also worked in the vineyard in the plant which processed grapes and exported them. And in 1992 I was sacked. We were 16 of us who were sacked then, and I had worked there for a long time, but then after I was sacked, I had to set up my own business and worked as a barber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was your barber's job?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was in the courtyard of my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the building where Milos Scekic worked?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, at the police station in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell me where the police station is in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. The police station in Prizren is closer to the courthouse, close to the Prizren-Gjakove Road, and it's a few hundred metres from the road which goes towards the Albanian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been in that building, and have you ever been in the office of Mr. Scekic?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I was there as well as the headmaster of the school of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get that part. Headmaster of the school in the village, does that mean that both of you went to his office or what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, because a few days before that, Milos Scekic came dressed in civilian clothes, and he had a bandaged left arm. He was together with another policeman but dressed in civilian clothes. He was called Denic. And Scekic asked me to call the headmaster and both with him to collect the weapons in the village. And I told him that I'm not in charge of the village, and I cannot command my own children, let alone the villagers. And he said I'm going to sends one of my children to go and call the headmaster, but they didn't allow him to go there. So we went there together. I was accompanied by them, and the name of the headmaster is Liman Thaqi. He wasn't in the house, so we were told to go there in the evening. And in the evening, I told him what the police Scekic had told us. And we called on the LDK leader -- a local leader Hysni Hoxha and also discussed the issue with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus on my question. I asked you if you had been to the office of Mr. Scekic. You said yes, and you mentioned the headmaster of the school in that context. So I asked you then if he was with you at the office of Mr. Scekic. And now before we clear that up, you began your answer by saying "because a few days before ..." Before what? Which time-period do you mean?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: A day before that, I remember it was as if yesterday, that is the following day in the morning, I went to the police station together with the headmaster. We had been asked to report to him, to go to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What time was it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I cannot remember the dates, but I had kept a record of the dates in my home, but the Serb police and military took every documentation that we had in the house. But it's approximately in August or September. I cannot exactly say what the date was. I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Talking about 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now tell me, how did you come into the office in were you able to simply walk into the police station and go to Milos Scekic's office, just like that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We travelled by bus to Prizren. It's about 4 kilometres. We went there, reported to the police station. We told them that we've been asked to by Scekic. There we met some villagers who were being detained at the police station. We also met Dragan who was working at the police station. I can't remember his other name. And we told him that we had been asked by Scekic to go to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Scekic was the third highest ranking man in SUP Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know. I knew he was a commander. That's what they called him, but what post he held, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how do you explain that he addressed you in relation to arms and that he put you in touch with the headmaster?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. Up until that moment, Scekic and his brother had been to my shop several times. As to why he addressed me, I don't know. And he told us that if you don't collect the weapons, then we'll set the whole village on fire, just like we've done in other villages. And when we went the next day to his office, he repeated the same words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And had he spoken to you before, and had you been to the police station before that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, I had never been there before. That was the first time that I had been to that police station. First and the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons with a licence?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, I've never carried any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone in your extended family have a licensed weapon?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Never. We've never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said you used to work in PIK Progress. Does PIK Progress have any barns close to your house?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you go on the Djakovica-Prizren Road in the direction of Prizren, does PIK Progress have any barns on the right side of the road?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, and there was also the headquarters of the building and the offices for the agriculture, for the vineyards, and for the management of the company. The offices were there; that's where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm interested in these barns. How far are they from your house?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Approximately, I haven't measured, but about a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I never expect you to give me exact distances. I'm interested in what you can tell me approximately. Is it true that a heap of weapons was left standing next to those barns in September of the year you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I haven't heard that, and I don't think that's true. That's all speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's what you think. And did you hear a public appeal to everyone in Kosovo and Metohija in September 1998 that they may hand in weapons, and they would be exempted from Prosecution for possessing weapons they have no licence for or possessing weapons for which licences are not issued at all?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I heard because they came with loud-speakers and armoured vehicles, the Serb police, I mean, and they called on the population to surrender their weapons, and the dead-line passed. It was one evening. And that evening all of the village left their homes, especially the women and children, and they left and they went to Prizren where they stayed for about ten days. And that was because they feared for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what were the men doing?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I couldn't see everyone, but my -- I had to stay with my brother in the house because he was handicapped. We stayed, both of us, in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. I had my military service in Srem Mitrovica. I served in the Yugoslav army and that was for 18 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was your specialty? Your military specialty?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I wasn't part of the infantry or any other force. I worked as a barber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And tell me, what schools did you finish?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I finished four years of regular schooling in Reti village. And at the time, we didn't have any books or any notebooks or any pens. After that, we moved to what was Dushanove village, and I had another four years of schooling there, and then I had another two years in the high school. And that was a private school because we didn't have other possibilities. So it's ten years altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You mean to tell me that until 1970, the year until which you were in school, you attended private schools? Or were you learning a trade?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, there was four elementary, four eighth-year school. And then we had another two years in the medical college, the high school college in Prizren. We had to pay to attend that. I can't remember how much we paid for that because it was a private school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A private secondary medical school in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was called the medical high school, but in fact it was a general high school. It was closer to the fountain and the Catholic church. Whether it exists there today, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that's a state-run secondary medical school? That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It -- then it was state owned, and probably today, if it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that country was called the socialist country, at least it called itself a socialist country and private schools did not exist until the 1990s of the past century?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I do not want any provocations. I didn't exactly want to say that it was a private school, but we went there privately. We paid to attend those courses. And it was the same rights to go to school whether one was a Serb or an Albanian or a Turk. We were entitled to go to school and do it on a part-time basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now about this column of people you told me about when you talked about the 28th of March. Were there any Turks in it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, there weren't any Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you served in the army, what kind of uniform did you have?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: One solid colour, SMB colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I see from the statement you had two sons. One was 19 in 1999, and your eldest son, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: My elder son was Bekim, he was about 20, 21 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your sons do their regular military service?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I've already asked you in which way Scekic put you in contact with the headmaster of the school. Were you perhaps politically active in 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, I was never involved in any political activity, but maybe thought because I had that barber's shop there I was the right person to get to the village and ask the people to surrender the weapons. Because they told me, you are the main person in the neighbourhood to which I responded I was not. But then we did call on the people to collect to the mosque and informed them that the police had told us that everyone should hand in their weapons otherwise we'd fare consequences. But I didn't hear that anyone had a weapon, actually, and I don't know whether someone handed it -- I think they didn't have any weapons, and they didn't surrender any weapons as far as I know. Maybe I couldn't guarantee 100 percent for each and every one, but in general I believed, and I still believe that people didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear that in the summer of 1998 there was some fighting in Kosova-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I heard. And I saw with my own eyes it in many places. If you want me, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm only interested in how this fighting was conducted, with what.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I said even earlier when I worked in the vineyards at Progress export Prizren for many years, the place called Landovica was a place where the Serbian army was stationed. They shelled from there in the direction of Vrini village which comprises, Hoqe, Lez, Belus, and some other villages above Prizren. In Suhareke municipality we saw they fired at the school. I have forgotten about the actual casualties, but I believe that some kids were killed in another village which was 2 kilometres away from ours. Cani [phoen] it was called which was, as the crow flies, not more than one, one and a half kilometres. The Serbian military tanks were stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are giving me very extensive answers, and I can't interrupt you. My question was with what kind of weapons was this fighting conducted, because you said there was fighting, that was the question. You haven't answered it. But tell me then, do you know if the KLA entered Orahovac on the 17th, 18th, July 1998.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me then about June 1998, did you go to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't remember for what reason. I don't know why you are asking me about Prishtina, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Because if you went to Pristina, I wanted to ask you which road did you take?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The road to Prishtina goes through Rahovec-Malisheve but also through Suhareke to Stimlje, Lipjan, and then you go to Prishtina. There's other two ways you can go to Prishtina, but I don't recall to have been to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Obviously you don't remember that you couldn't take that road at the time you had to go via Strpce and take the partisan road via Strecka [phoen] and Nerodimlje to get to Pristina; but since you didn't go to Pristina, it's no use talking about it. You also haven't heard, have you, that the Pristina-Pec Road was blocked in 1998?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't remember that because, as I said, I didn't go there myself, so I don't want to say something that I didn't see or experience myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You've said many things that you have not seen or experienced yourself but only heard from others. Tell me, how did you know who headed the DSK in your village?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: When the LDK branch, LDK for Kosova was founded, headed by the late Ibrahim Rugova, there was a party called LDK. And we voted in our village for Hysni Hoxha as the chairman of the LDK branch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was this voting?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, but I think it was about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you vote for anyone else except for the DSK?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Maybe there would have been other persons eligible for that, but we believe that he was the best choice because he had had a legal background. And so we found him to be the best candidate for the LDK in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the DSK's platform?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Briefly, I would say it was a peaceful platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I believe that you can't reach anything resorting to bad means and to violence. I think you can do everything through a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was their goal, irrespective of the means?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You started explaining that one needs to use peaceful means to reach one's goal, in this case the party platform and its objectives. And I was asking you about that; what was their goal?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The goal of this party was that everyone resort to a peaceful way and that war it averted. But Kosovars couldn't avoid the war because, as you know, we were subjected to a lot of maltreatment. You know very well that even during the Yugoslav army time, many Albanian soldiers were killed. I don't want to go into this kind of debate because I'm not a politician, but your question made me give this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm kindly asking you to answer briefly. What was the goal of the DSK? You keep on discussing the means, but you did not answer -- you didn't tell me what the goal of the party was.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: LDK and the entire Albanian people who embrace and supported LDK wanted to resort to a peaceful road. I don't know what kind of other answer you expect from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I expect of you to tell me where that peaceful road was supposed to take you.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. When was it that you heard of the KLA for the first time?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was about sometime in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was it that you heard about the activities of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I heard that the Liberation Army of Kosova was formed which would strive for Kosova's independence, but I didn't see any of its activities with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, you were in no position to see what their activities were, since you did not participate in them. I'm asking you this though: What means did the KLA use in order to reach their objective?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know, and I didn't see what means they had. Because in my village Dushanove, which is no longer called so, there were no KLA soldiers. So I can't give you any further answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that there were no KLA soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There weren't because I didn't see any in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what KLA members look like?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them through television.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you describe them?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Like an army, they had camouflage uniforms. They had the logo of the Kosova Liberation Army with an eagle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which TV station did you see that on?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I saw it on Belgrade television, Novi Sad, and on Prishtina channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was broadcast about KLA activities and the way they operated?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The Belgrade television at that time broadcast that these are terrorists, but in fact, it was a liberation army of Kosova by liberated Kosova also thanks to the assistance of the international community and NATO liberating all its people irrespective of the ethnicities. When we were driven out of Kosova and after their intervention, we could return back to our homes. And this was done in cooperation with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Around what time did you see the information you refer to as having seen it on television?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Sometime in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you find out that your younger son attended training with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There is a misunderstanding or misinterpretation. I don't know whether it was my fault or the interpreters. He was not a member of the KLA, but he was in the part where the army was because he was sought by the police. And he went to find shelter with his aunt in Drenac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P876 in the Albanian and English versions, para 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please read out paragraph number 2 on this page of the statement out loud.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. "The only person from my family who was involved with the KLA was my younger son Agrim Kryeziu, 19 years old, who was exercising/training with the KLA for a few days last year when the Serb attack started last spring, 1998. From September 1998, he decided to leave the country and go to Germany for safety reasons. He is still living in Germany now, in Dusseldorf, and I don't know his address or telephone number because he calls me from a post office there."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you provided this statement it was read back to you in Albanian; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You signed it afterwards, signing the English version?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: At that time we were in Albania, and I didn't know where my elder son and daughter were. When I gave this statement, I'm sure that they may have misunderstood me when I said in the part of the KLA. Actually, I didn't pay much attention to it, because I was very worried about my family members, but he was not a member. I would have wished he was a member because it was a regular liberation army, but he was not in fact. And that's why I'm saying a mistake may have been made here. Either it's my fault or the interpreters fault, but I simply said where the KLA is exercising, in that part he is. He went there for security reasons, I mean, because he felt safer there. He was sought by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said you would have been happy had he been a member of the KLA, since the KLA was a regular liberation army. Can you tell me something about the way that liberation army operated?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I said earlier, I was not a member. And I was never in that part where it operated to see what it was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since you were not a member of theirs and you were not in any area where they were active, perhaps you can still tell me something about the things you heard about the way they operated?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I heard that they fought with the police or the army of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that they possessed any weapons?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I heard and I also saw on television that they had some automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the reason why people were being invited in September 1998, announcing it over loud-speakers in Kosovo that people should surrender their arms and that in that case they would not be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The people in general didn't have weapons. The army had. The liberation army of Kosova had to fight with the army of the former Yugoslavia, the Serbian army, but not to fight against elderly women 90 years old, or our kids of 7 or 8 or so years old. It's always the case that an army fights another army, not against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we are now discussing P877. On the 19th of September, 2004, you gave a statement to the Prosecutor's Office of The Hague Tribunal. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. They must have been in my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you corrected certain things from the statement you had given on the 14th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't remember what change you are referring to. Maybe you can explain to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P877.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the front page of the statement. It says the 19th of September, 2004. I don't think you have it in hard copy; you'll have to follow on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the court clerk to display page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you see the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Is it on the left or on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, we'll go back to it. But look at the body of the statement. It is rather short. What was the correction that you made?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Probably it was the correction about the number of the houses. From 120, it should be about 1.200.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you did not enter any other corrections. Having given the original statement five years prior to that, the only correction you had to make concerned the number of houses in Dusanovo; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn now for the first break and resume at 11.00. We'll have a break now, and the court officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the right-hand side of the screen you see you said at the time it was all stated to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was five years after the first statement. Let me ask you now, where is the Denj village?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The Denj village is on the road Prizren-Gjakove somewhere beyond the Xerxe village. There is Gradishte, Rakoc [phoen], and then you go to Denj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you turn off to the right from the road to Djakovica in the direction of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, in Xerxe you turn right to go to Rahovec, then you travel another kilometre and then you turn right to Gradishte before you go to the holy bridge and then the first village is Gexhe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This that village, where was the KLA training camp?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know that. In Denj there was a KLA base, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I know the area very well, but I have never heard of Denj village until I read the supplemental information you gave to the Prosecution in 2006. And you mentioned this village Denj saying that there was a KLA training camp there.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's not true that I've said that, and it's not true that there was a training camp of the KLA there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I always trust the Prosecution, especially when they give me things in writing. It was an interview with you on the 23rd of November, I suppose here in The Hague. On the eve of your testimony in the Milutinovic case, that was a correction you made. And it's on the record. You have to take my word for it. It's now on the record in this case and in that one. But let me ask you, did you have a relative in that camp when your son was leaving regardless of whether he was in the KLA or not?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, there was no camp in my village, and I did not have -- I did not have any relatives there in Denj, but I've always described how we were maltreated. You always avoid asking me questions about how people were maltreated, how they were killed, and how they were fired upon. But you should ask me questions about what I've said in the statement. I don't know that there was such a camp of the KLA in Denj, and I haven't touched on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please believe me, I may get things wrong sometimes, but I never deliberately tell untruths. I have already explained this. Let's move on, and we'll come to your statement. You keep repeating things from your witness statement, that's why I'm not asking you about it. You always keep telling me the same thing over and over again regardless of what my question is. But please focus on my questions, answer them briefly and to the point so that we finish quickly. You have experience with prior trials. This Trial Chamber will allow me as much time as I need in view of your answers. The same rules as before will not necessarily apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call up P318.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you allow me to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As long as I live, what I have experienced I have said and I will say every time I'm given the opportunity to say what I've experienced and what I've seen with my very own eyes. And I still see that as something which is going through my mind's eye, all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Djurdjic, if you would carry on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, on this picture, can you recognise anything?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Number 1, it's a tank; an armoured vehicle at number 2. And the third and the fourth, I cannot identify them very well. But -- but I can very well remember number 1 and number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who had the vehicle under number 1?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was also the police had such armoured vehicles, but number 2 was specifically used by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what colour is number 1?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We call it green.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the colour of the uniform of the soldier protruding from the turret?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It's a mono-colour uniform, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which colour?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It's the same colour as the armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What do you see on this picture, Witness?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Number 6 is the military tanks. And number 5 were police vehicles. And number 7 is a Pinzgauer. And I haven't seen the number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which colour is number 7?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That was the colour of the Pinzgauers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is any of these vehicles familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I can't remember very well. I'm focusing on the 10, but I cannot see very well what kind of vehicle it is. Some police forces used similar vehicles, but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what is the colour of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: In the picture you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: A kind of green in this particular picture. It's a kind of green colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, tell me, where was the house of Haki Cuni?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Haki Cuni's house was about a hundred metres further away from my house. It was in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it along the road Prizren-Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, it's in the entrance of the Dushanove village. It's on the transit road, and it's about 2- to 300 metres away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Haki Cuni's occupation?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: He was the driver of the director of PIK Progress, export Prizren, the company where I worked. He was a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You stated that you had heard he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I heard from his family when I paid a visit there. The police had told them that he was killed, but fortunately, he was found alive and released on the 12th or 13th of September when the NATO troops moved in. He was -- he was tied hand and feet and his mouth was also taped, and when they found him in a lorry, at the back of a lorry. And he was part of a group of another 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was from one of his brothers, a member of his family. That's what the police, the Serb police had told them, that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please listen to my question carefully. When -- at what time did you hear he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I heard before we were forced to leave our houses and go towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean before the 28th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I made my statement, and I said there that it was a month before that. But when we came back from Albania and Haki Cuni was released, then I heard that he was released and he was alive, and on the 19th of March, I saw him with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that in June 1999 you heard he was alive?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you made a correction to your statement, as we have seen before, on the 19th of September, 2004, and you did not execute that correction.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that regarding Haki Cuni? Is that regarding Haki Cuni? That there have been corrections?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, it was confirmed that Haki Cuni was alive on the 12th or 13th of June when NATO moved in. He was released from the back of a lorry where he was tied hands and feet, and his mouth was taped. And it was the German KFOR forces that released him and another group of people. And he was alive. I returned on the 17th of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: -- from Albania to my house in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The interpretation you are receiving is excellent. Please answer my question. I just put it to you that in 2004 you made a supplemental statement. We've seen that statement. You made only one correction in that supplemental information regarding the number of houses in Dusanovo. I'm telling you that in 2004, you did not make a correction regarding this gentleman we are discussing, Haki Cuni.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: If I was asked, I will have corrected it just like you are asking me. But you have the example of my wife who died in -- around about that time, so I wasn't very much focused because I had that grievance in my family, that bereavement in my family. And if I was asked, I would have corrected the facts, put the facts straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but was it the most important thing to make a corrigendum to your statement from 1999 as to whether there were 120 houses in Dusanovo or more?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were about 1.200 houses, and not 120 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, will you agree with me that when you heard the testimony of Mr. Ognjenovic, Nebojsa Ognjenovic, that he had talked on the phone with Haki Cuni, that's when you decided to make a corrigendum, and that's how you testified in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's not true. I don't know that Nebojsa has spoken to Haki Cuni, and I haven't stated any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that from the testimony of Nebojsa Ognjenovic you heard he had talked to Haki Cuni and that the latter was alive. And you corrected yourself in the Milutinovic case accordingly. That's when you said for the first time that Haki Cuni was alive?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No. I didn't know whether Nebojsa had spoken to Haki Cuni, I only heard from Haki Cuni's family. And for the duration of the time that we were in Albania, we knew that Haki Cuni was dead, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You obviously do not wish to answer my question in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, that's not a fair comment. You have one view of the facts. The witness is trying to tell you another. You are not accepting his answer. So it's not proper for you to say, You are not wanting to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I put to him the 1999 and 2004 statements and for the first time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that. The only issue is why he didn't make a change in 2004. You have one version that it's because of evidence that was given later. His answer is: I wasn't asked about it in 2004. Because of the death of my wife I wasn't worried about these things. I made an alteration to the number of houses increasing it from 120 to 1.200 because I was asked about it. I wasn't asked about anything else. Now, that may be right or it may be wrong. You've put to him that that is wrong and there's another reason. He says no. I think you better move on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall when Prizren was bombed for the first time?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No, not Prizren. It was the military barracks that was bombed on the 24th of March about 2000, 2015, on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where is the barracks that was bombed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The barracks of Serbia Yugoslavia in Prizren is located on the road Prizren-Suhareke at the exit of Prizren where now is the German KFOR; other forces, I don't know. That was the place where it was stationed, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From that moment until when you departed, was there any fighting around Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, I know and I stated earlier that from the vineyard where I worked for many years called Landovice where the forces of the Serbian army were stationed and from where they bombed -- shelled Vrinje, set fire to the houses, the part of Suhareke, Rahovec, from there they shelled. These fightings I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It happened from 1998 until 28th of March at 1700 hours where we were -- when we were forced to flee from our own homes by the Serbian forces. And on the way to Albania, we saw Vrinje being set fire to, some other villages like Zhur, Nebrusht. When we was walking, it was night. We had a blanket over our shoulders. We saw people being beaten up, maltreated, warn out from walking and from what was going on. But everyone was worried to save his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Between the 24th and the 28th of March of 1999, whether you know if there was any fighting around Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We heard that on the 24th of March we heard the NATO strikes against the Yugoslav barracks at 2000 hours or so that I mentioned, but the shelling by the Yugoslav army continued all day long against these villages that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 24th of March as you say, were you in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the distance from Dusanovo to Landovica?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Dushanove is near from the transit road where my house is about 5 kilometres, I would say, from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how far is it from Dusanovo to Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: From Dushanove to Suhareke it is about 18 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you say that the KLA was not in the vicinity of Dusanovo. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I know this because I didn't see them with my eyes, by this I mean that there was no fighting between the Serb military forces or police forces and them. There was no fighting around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand your answer, on the 24th, you were in your home in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you leave Dusanovo at any point?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the 25th, did you leave Dusanovo then?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We didn't dare leave the village for fear of the Serb forces because every time we were stopped by them, we were maltreated, beaten up, or taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you leave Dusanovo on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How can you say then that you know there was no fighting with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There was no fighting I said because I saw with my own eyes the tanks of the Serb Yugoslav army in the place called -- vineyard in Landovice. And I also saw them shelling because as the crow flies the place was not more than one or one and a half kilometres from where I lived. I could see from my own house everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You saw the tank, but was it engaging anyone?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I already said, the tanks were simply shelling the villages, Vrinje which comprises Hoqe, Belus, Lez, some villages which I can't remember the names of now. The part of Rahovec -- we could see the flames coming out of the houses or the smoke from where we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say you saw shells land in all of these villages?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: When they shelled, we could see the flames or the smoke coming out of the houses. They didn't fight with the KLA, they fought with the Kosova innocent, unarmed inhabitants. The same of the police and Army of Yugoslavia was to drive out the population from Kosova. I already said that they yelled at us, they slandered our -- cursed our mothers, they said go to Albania, go to Thaqi, go to Clinton. You belong to Albania, Kosova is Serbia, and these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that there was no KLA presence in the villages you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know because I was not a member myself and I didn't see any fighting between the Serb military or police and the KLA, but I only saw the military and police tanks shelling, bombing. Because we saw, as I said, the flames, the fire coming out. And through the information outlets, we heard that such and such number of people were injured or killed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but if one goes from Dusanovo to Djakovica you have to go across a hill following which there is Landovica; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was a monument of Boro and Ramiz at the time of the former Yugoslavia. Now we have the hero cemetery there, you are correct. Yes that road goes to Gjakove, and this is where Landovice is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct that both Dusanovo and the Prizren depression or field --

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- is towards Prizren itself? In your statement it says you went to your cousin's house. His name is Agim. Did I understand correctly that it was actually your own brother rather than a cousin of yours?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: When the Serb forces entered on the 28th of March at about 5.00 in the afternoon, the road is about 8 metres wide and 2 kilometres long; there are several intersections there. I couldn't go to my house. I entered the house of Agim Kryeziu who is my first cousin and at that moment the Serb military and police forces entered his house with masks and they took away some money from his mother. And there I saw these forces beating people, and I saw Nebi Bucaj taken away because we all live in the same area close by to each other. And the women were being maltreated. I heard shots being fired from all over the place with all sorts of weaponry. And as I said, they kept yelling at us, cursing us, leave your houses, go to Albania. They curse our mothers. I saw Abdurrahman Ahmetaj which -- who lived near Shukac [phoen] being beaten by the police together with his son Besnik was covered in blood until he fainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No one did anything to you; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Me personally, no. But my wife, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are still in the house and the yard of Agim Kryeziu?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your wife was not in his yard?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No. She was at home, in the house we lived together, about 20, 30 metres away from Agim's. We were in the same courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The yard of your house, was it enclosed by a wall? Was there a wall?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, we had a wall, but it was not a tall wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was it made of?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was made of concrete blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a gate?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the height of the gate, and what was the gate made of?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The door was made of iron. It was about 2 metres, 2 metres and 20 centimetres high, and 4 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you arrived in your cousin's yard, where were you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I was in the street near my house and Agim's house. There is a transformer there, and we were talking among ourselves. Because of the 27th of March in the afternoon, the police forces had driven out of Mamushe village all the people -- all its population, and we could see them passing by in tractor, walking on foot, women crying with children. Among them were also my sister and her brother, and she said, Where are they? I don't know where they are taking us. And I said, I don't know. And this happened on the 27th of March, 1999. So we were there for a couple of minutes. On the 28th then a white jeep or Niva came near the house of Fadil and Safet Kryeziu, and we entered Agim's house. In a minute, I don't know, as if they sprang up from the ground, the house was filled with military and police forces. And they broke down the doors and fired at the houses in all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I conclude then, that on the 28th of March, that is to say before that morning, you did not leave your house or the yard?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I didn't leave the house because we didn't dare leave the house because there were so many check-points maybe every 100 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I said that morning, but I meant to say before 4.00 p.m. on the 28th of March, you did not leave your house, did you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's correct, but I went out to the street and met neighbours or friends and talked. But whenever we saw forces coming by, we went inside because they always directed their weapons to us and cursed our Albanian mothers as if that was the most normal thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The transformer station you mentioned is quite close to your house; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's correct. It is closer to my cousin's house, but also close to my house. 50, 60 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you wear the traditional Albanian head-gear?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the people you spoke to, did they wear it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Some did, especially the elderly people. Some of them do even now, and they will always wear these skull caps because it's part of our national costume. Usually the young people don't wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that. It is usually the elderly from rural areas that wear such caps, but younger people and people living in urban areas usually do not; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There are some persons who wear them, some don't. I never wore it. No one in my family wears such a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Dusanovo there were Serb families, as you mentioned, and you specified several Serb last names. If one went down a street in such an environment, how could you tell one person from the next in terms of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I gave my statement, and I abide by it, that about 20 Serbian households, I couldn't know all of them, they were Serbs and Montenegrins. Until that time before the war started in Kosova, we got on well together with the Serbs. We didn't have any problems. We respected each other. If there were 200 Albanians and 2 Serbs working in the same place, we used to speak Serbian even though they knew Albanian but they never spoke Albanian, but we did speak Serbian. We respected them as a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Please listen carefully to my questions. Everything you said so far in all the statements and transcripts is something we have before us. We are familiar with those. I simply want to put questions to you which had not been asked of you until now. I'm not interested in anything else, the rest is before the Chamber. My question is, how could someone like the police or the forces that were in your village tell which nationality or of which ethnic background you are?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
