utterances.text: Yes, because all the Serbs in the village of former -- called Dushanove now Urbana [phoen] were members in the army and the police of Serbia. Some days earlier, they removed their families from the village because they knew that something was going to happen. So they expected fighting, but we, being unarmed, being in a position to do nothing, were forced to leave the house being subjected to beating, maltreatment, robbing, and all this. And all this happened -- was done by the Serb police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are trying to tell me that Milos Scekic and Nebojsa Ognjenovic did not live in their houses?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: During those days they must not have lived there because they knew what was going to happen. Because we too as I said were afraid to leave our houses even some days prior to what happened. And we saw many neighbours dressed in police uniforms. People whom we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I conclude then that it is your presumption that Scekic and Ognjenovic moved out?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty because those two lived further down, but Petkovic was -- lives closer to me, and he left with his house. His son too was mobilised in the police. Stanisa Petkovic also. Because I saw them in police uniforms, all my neighbours were mobilised in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The police were tasked with the regular policing duties, but in their spare time they must have lived in their homes?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I already said that they were not regular police. They were police who wanted to beat Albanians, to kill them, to force them to flee their territories. We see policemen everywhere, but they behave in a normal way. Of course they have their policing duties, but it's not part of their duties, I suppose, to beat people, to violate people, to rob people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that when you discuss those policemen, you do not have in mind regular active-duty policemen in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I already said these were civilians, and were drafted, mobilised by the government of Serbia either with their own will or forced to do so, and they were used against Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What kinds of uniforms did you see on the 20th while you were still in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We saw dark blue police uniforms. We saw SMB colour uniform and camouflage uniform. I saw people dressed in black uniforms, people wearing beards, long hair, with those caps called "sajkaca," with Chetniks' kokards, with long bloody knives. And this reminded me the movie of Draza Mihailovic, and I thought that the Chetniks were back in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The people in black uniforms, were you able to see their insignia?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I saw only the kokards. Their black kokards, the kokardas of Chetniks, long beards, long hair, and the bloody knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you please describe of what material this cockade was made of and what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Haven't worked in that factory where they are produced, I never managed to touch it. They were very sad to see on those people's heads. They were terrifying us. They were putting knives to our throats. Ask experts in those factories where they were produced, they will tell you exactly what they were made of. There are people in Serbia to this day that wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you were in the army, what kind of cap did you wear?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Used to wear the caps of the former Yugoslav army. They were normal army caps, and there was a star on the cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I've never heard of any factory making cockades. But please describe the cockade to me, because I can't understand what kind of cap you are talking about. I also watched movies like you did, I know what they looked like during the World War II. But tell me, what did those caps look like, and what is it that you call cockade?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I've seen that cockade earlier in the film by Draza Mihailovic. They had exactly the same uniform, the same cockades, the same uniforms; and I thought that Draza Mihailovic was back in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What kind of insignia did you see on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: As I said, I wasn't focused to watch the details, what signs, what emblems were on those cockades; but I knew that those black cockades were part of the Chetnik uniforms. I said, I remember that it was exactly the same as the cockades and uniforms that I saw in the field. I haven't had the opportunity to handle that cockade. To see what it feels like and what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I stopped asking you about cockades. I'm not asking you about cockades anymore, I'm asking you about insignia. Are there any differences between the cockade and the uniform?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Wearing black uniforms, long beards, cockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned seeing several uniforms, I'm asking you if you had seen -- noticed some insignia on those uniforms, and if you did, what kind?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I saw on the left-hand side they had the writing Beli Orlovi, White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see any other insignia?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Maybe I've seen, but it's ten years since I last saw them, and I can't remember anything else other than Beli Orlovi, which I've seen myself. And I wasn't any more interested in the detail, but how to save myself, the life of my family, my brother, my nieces and nephews, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you left the yard of this relative of yours, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I took my car and my brother who is handicapped, and his son, and the whole family; and we set out. I popped out of the car to lock the doors of my house, but the police put the weapons to my head and said don't lock the doors to your house. And then they got into the house and looted everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, let's go step by step when you answer my questions. You left the house of your relative and got to your own house. Did you go into your own house? Just answer yes or no, I have to finish this.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I told my wife, let's get out and leave. She started crying and the children were crying, the women were crying. I told them, Don't cry, we will slowly get out of here. Nothing will happen to us. But then we heard gun-shots, and as I wanted to lock the doors into my house, I was not allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were there any police in your yard when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There were police everywhere. They broke the gates of the houses with tanks, armoured vehicles, whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please answer my questions straightforwardly. When you came to your own yard, were there any police there or soldiers, whoever?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: At that moment, no, but the doors were open. They came to the door, they were calling names on us. But in the courtyard of the Kryeziu, yes, they were there. It was in the courtyard of Agim Kryeziu. We lived in the same compound, although we had our separate households as of 1975. However, there are about seven houses in the same compound. We share the same property, the same land.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you and Agim share the same yard?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It was a territory of 42 acres, and Agim Kryeziu had his own courtyard and we had ours; and it was like 50 metres distance between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was there a wall between your yard and Agim's?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we finally established that the police did not -- or rather, these forces, these troops who were there, did not enter your yard?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: They were at the gates of my courtyard because we share the same alleyway, the three brothers. The gates were open, and they were out there calling names on us and shouting and yelling, telling us, Get out, go to Albania, that's where you belong, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is your garage within your yard?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: The garage is at the entrance by the main road as you enter into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who else got into the car with you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I didn't know where my son Bekim was and his wife. I didn't know where my daughter was. It was my wife who got on, my mother-in-law, and there were some other people from Bellacerke, they were friends who had come over, they were mostly women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many of you got into that car?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether it was four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you set out in that car; right?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when you got the car out of the yard, you stopped?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: So went on to the main transit road. I popped out of the car to close the gates and the doors into the house, but I was threatened not to. Then I went back into the car. And within 500 metres, the police stopped us. That's where we were threatened, our cars were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: My brother's car as well was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where were your sons and daughter and your daughter-in-law?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: My son and his wife went to their uncle's in Prizren. There was a fear. Whereas my daughter who was married, she is in Ortokol -- she was in Ortokol. When they took my car, they also asked me about the -- where my son was, Bekim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is the check-point where you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: It wasn't a check-point. I told you that the road is about 2 kilometres, and it's 18 metres wide. On both sides there were masked policemen and soldiers; and near the house of Milos Scekic, there where we were also beating Ahmetaj, Abdurrahman Ahmetaj. There they stopped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, did you go out on to the main road, Prizren-Djakovica, with your car?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We were not allowed to get there. We were not allowed to get to the Prizren-Gjakove road, but we were stopped on the road which is the transit road that goes towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you say you were stopped by the police there? Or it wasn't the police. Who stopped you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Everybody was masked, policemen and soldiers, as well as those that I -- the Chetniks I described earlier with the cockades and the black uniforms and the long beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was on those men in camouflage? What colour?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Are you talking about the Serb police and army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the camouflage uniforms you just mentioned. I'm asking you what colour they were. I don't know who was wearing them.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: There were people wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the design on them?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I haven't touched them, and I don't know about the design or who made them. All I know is that they were camouflage uniforms. You can ask those who produced them about the design.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see any insignia on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Maybe there were symbols, there were insignia. I saw some which were the Beli Orlovi. But there was no time for us to think and watch and observe these details because we were fearing for our lives, we were being beaten up, we were being looted, and we had no time to focus on what insignia they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that you did not even dare look sideways in fear of these people?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We didn't dare to turn our heads and look behind us for a long time, but obviously we could see around us who was there and what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were not able to distinguish the colour of the uniform or the insignia. Tell me, why did you stop after 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We were stopped by the police. They had pointed the gun to my brother's head and his son. I stopped there, and I addressed the Milos Scekic who was wearing a stocking -- a lady's stocking on his head and told him, Please, commander, leave us -- allow us to have a car because my brother is handicapped, and he cannot walk. And my wife opened the boot to take something, and they hit her with the butt of their automatic weapons, and she fainted. I was lucky to have a bottle of water in the car, and some people there helped us to revive her. And my brother who was handicapped was taken to Prizren in a car. He had only one leg. And then we carried on with our journey and travelled all night long, all night through until we reached Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your brother have his own family? Was he married with children?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did he have his wife and children with him?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. His elder brother -- his elder son, a nephew, his daughter-in-law, and there was also a young child who we had to carry all the way up until we reached Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your brother's wife in the car with you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From your house to the border, you said there were 40 kilometres. How long did it take you to cover that distance?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: That's exactly what I've said, but I haven't measured the distance. We walked all the night from 5.00 in the afternoon until the next morning. And it's roughly about 40 kilometres, and that's according to the assessment of people who have travelled that road before. So we walked for about 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You confused me a bit now. Did you reach the Prizren-Djakovica road at all?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't -- I didn't confuse you, but you confused yourself. We came out to the school of the village, that's where we were allowed to take the road towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you get out onto the main road at all, the Prizren-Djakovica road?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know whether you are understanding me. We went to the school of the village then. Then we were allowed to go to the main road towards Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. So you did come to the main road. Now, going on the main road, how did you continue? Did you turn right into the industrial zone and use the roundabout way to get to the intersection with Putnik Hotel on it?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We continued on the main road because we did not dare to divert our road. And there is an industrial zone there, and there are some companies there, Printex, Famipa [phoen]. There there was a group of policemen, and we saw them maltreating people. And they stopped the cars, and they beat people up. And up until Zhur we saw the police on both sides and they were travelling on the opposite side. In Zhur there was the check-point. And the next one was on the border with Albania, Vermice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How wide is the Prizren-Djakovica road?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I haven't measured, but around 6 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How wide is the road in the industrial zone?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I haven't measured, but it's about 7 to 8 metres, or 6. I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The road from Prizren to Vrmnica, the border crossing, is it the same width?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I don't know. I already said that I am not an expert and I haven't measured the roads. But I can tell you about where I lived, so that's where I have better knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you driving?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I drove the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go by car on this road towards the border?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Maybe we've been out to Vermice to have the fish. There was a place that cooked very good fish in Vermice. We had the money, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you drive on that road?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That column you were in, did it occupy the whole road?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes, the column occupied the whole road. They were all elderly, women, children. They were older people, up to 100 years old, and there were people who needed assistance. This does not appear to have happened anywhere else in the world. I hope it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from Zur, did you go the same way to the border crossing from the intersection towards Zur or towards Vrmnica? Did you move in the same way in?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: We followed the same road from Zhur to Vermice. But along the way, they had put up large concrete blocks, so we had to go through -- some people were saying that we had better not cross over that -- to the other area behind the concrete blocks because the Serbs will have mined that area, so we were all in a dilemma.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you went on that road towards the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, you recognised Milos Scekic although he was wearing a stocking on his head?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised him, and I spoke to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the Prizren police station confirmed to you that it was him wearing a stocking on his head?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: I knew him very well because I had lived with him in the same village for 40 years. Some soldiers and some other persons with beards said to me, Shut up or else you will be executed. Get off your car. But I said I could recognise him because he was wearing this lady's stocking, brown in colour. I could tell his face. I could recognise his voice. Even nowadays if I see him, I would be able to recognise him because, as I said, we've lived together for 40 years in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did he have anything on his head?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Most probably a head-gear on top of the stocking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My last question: What kind of uniform was Nebojsa Ognjenovic wearing?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: Nebojsa had a police uniform. I saw him at the customs office on the border with Albania. We had a conversation in Albanian. He asked me about my car, where my car was. And at the border, I saw how they confiscated cars, identification documents. They would throw these documents on some bins or tear them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the colour of that uniform?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI KRYEZIU
utterances.text: They are normal police uniform, in one solid colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Witness, I have no more questions. I have completed my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Yes, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can just indicate I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar, thank you. You'll be pleased to know that completes the questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give us. We know it's not your first visit; we are grateful that you've come more than once. You may now, of course, return to your normal activities, and we will study your evidence in due course. Thank you, sir. The court officer will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is obviously an appropriate occasion for the second break. We will resume at 5 minutes past 1.00. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next witness will be Mr. Hani Hoxha. Your Honours, while we are waiting, I can just mention, I know an issue has been raised regarding the Milosevic transcript which was not in the notification list, the exhibits to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The transcript is now added to the list, and I will seek to tender it, and the Defence counsel has already been notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your prayers are answered. Good afternoon, Mr. Hoxha. Will you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name and birth date for the record?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: My name is Hani Hoxha. I was born on the 16th of May, 1937, in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Before we start, I understand that you are wearing those dark glasses out of medical reasons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: You said you were born in Djakovica. Do you still live in this village?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on the 22nd of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read through this statement before you came to court today?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the information in the statement is a correct reflection of what you remembered happened in 1999?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Then I seek to tender this statement from 22nd of April, 1999, with the 65 ter number 02230 into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00879, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, did you also testify in the Milosevic trial on the 3rd July, 2002; and in the Milutinovic et al. case on the 11th of August, 2006?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And have you been given a chance to review those transcripts with a language assistant before you came to the court?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions as you were back then, would you provide the same answer today?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Then I seek it to tender those transcript into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will each be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, 65 ter numbers 02231 for the Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00880, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And the transcript of the Milutinovic et al. case is 65 ter number 05059.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00881, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I will now read out the court summary for this witness. The witness has testified that the local Serb villagers in Djakovica and surrounding areas formed a civic defence unit 1 to 2 months prior to the NATO bombing in March 1999. This civic defence which harassed and intimidated the local Albanian residents was, according to the witness, not formed by local initiative, but by the Yugoslavian government. The civic defence unit wore slightly different blue uniforms than the MUP. On or about 27th of March, 1999, the witness observed houses being burned and shots fired in his neighbourhood, Culak quarter. The Serb police tried to enter his gate, but they did not succeed and instead they entered his neighbour's house, killed the owner of the house Shefqet Pruti and then set the house on fire. The police then went to another neighbour of the witness, Avni Ferizi, broke through his gate and shot the owner of the house dead. Ferizi's family went to the local police to report the murders and were told to go and complain to NATO. The police retrieved and buried the bodies. The witness moved his family to the basement of the Vejsa home at Milos Gilic street in Djakovica as he believed it would be safe there. On the night of the 1st of April, the Serb police began breaking the gate of this house. The men decided to flee, thinking the women and children would not be harmed. The witness stayed in the area long enough to see 8 to 10 armed attackers, some wearing masks. He heard gun-shots and saw houses being burned. On 2nd of April, he went back to Vejsa home where he had fled from, and he found the house burned to the ground. He also found the witness Dreni Caka, 12 years old at that time, who told the witness that the attackers had killed all the women who were staying in the house, his own and the witness's female family members included. Later that day, the witness left Djakovica in a 3 kilometre long convoy of Kosovar Albanian civilians. The VJ transported the elderly and the infirm to the border by tractor. The witness was forced to give up his identity documents by MUP. And this is the end of the court summary. While we are waiting for the translation to be completed, could we please have up 65 ter number 00275 on the screen, which is an aerial photo of Djakovica. It's supposed to be a picture with the 65 ter number 00275. Thank you. If you can just zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, in your statement from 1999 you have explained how you took your family to the basement of the Vejsa home of the Milos Gilic Street in Djakovica because you believed it would be safe there. I would now like you to circle around the house that you moved into where you stayed with several other people in this street. And the usher will assist you with a pen.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: This house here with this white wall and this window was the bar of my son-in-law Lulzim Vejsa. In the basement of this house were sheltered 21 persons, my late wife and two daughters. In this other part here --

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, Mr. Hoxha. Could you please draw a larger circle around this house so it's easier for us to see.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, if you could just put a number 1 in that, and then you can continue with what you are about to explain.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: In this facility here in the basement, the entrance is from behind, were sheltered 21 persons on the night of the event. I, my son-in-law Luli and his son-in-law Behar stayed in this house within the same yard. You cannot see that house here because it was taken after that house was burnt. We stayed here trying to keep guard, so to say, because I believe you have read my statement and some events had taken place before which gave us the impression the situation was not a good one. It was in fact a serious one. It was night, there was no electricity. At about 12.00 midnight my son-in-law came. I was lying fully dressed, and he woke me up and said that the situation seemed very grave. I woke up my son-in-law Luli and Behar, went in a direction that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hoxha. I'm going to stop you there. So the house that you have circled, is it correct that this -- in this basement was the bar or the shop that you have explained in your statement also?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: This is where the store is. It's a store; it's not a house. It's a pool place. There are two shops here, whereas the dwelling house is this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: The dwelling house, could you please also mark a circle on that one.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The dwelling house used to be here. You can't see it in this picture; I'm putting a 2 here. This is where I stayed, in that dwelling house where I spent that critical night. The night where this tragedy occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And is it correct that the other one -- other people spent the night in the basement of the number 1 circle?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: How many people were there approximately, or maybe you remember accurate, how many people spent the night there?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The number of people who spent the night there was exactly 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And were there other people except your family who spent the night there?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes, there were. My wife, my daughter -- unmarried daughter. There was my married daughter Tululi with her five kids, her mother-in-law. There was Fetije's daughter, the owner of the house with her three children. There was another woman with three children. There was Fetije's brother Hysen Gashi was his name. And another family, a woman from Caka family with her three daughters and a son.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would also like you to draw a circle around the place that you were hiding during the attack of this house as you have described also in your statement.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact place but approximately, if I'm not mistaken, must be somewhere here. I'll put a question mark here to indicate that I'm not certain because it was night, and I never went back to that place. Because each time I go past that place, I feel very bad because you can -- very uncomfortable. You can imagine how one can feel after losing the wife and the children. So it's not with pleasure that I walk past this place. I may err on the side of 2 or 3 metres, but approximately this circle here shows the place where I was hiding on that critical night.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And for how long did you hide in this place?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: We stayed there until dawn. When it dawned, I came out of that place, there were two walls and a narrow gap between the two. I thought it would lead me somewhere out; but when I found another wall at the end of the alley, I stayed there for another six hours. I can't remember exactly. But when the security forces who conducted the massacre left, then I came out of that place. And there I was joined by a neighbour from the same area. And then we went to the house we were in initially, and when I -- when we went back there, I noticed that Luli's house was burned to the ground. Then I went to the basement where I saw the bodies of my -- I went to find my wife and daughters and other people who were in there, but I didn't find anyone. I thought they had left and then went to another room where another uncle of Luli's lived. There I saw the body. And at that point, I started thinking of the worst. And when we came to the house where we lived, as it was burned to the ground, the neighbour who joined me, they saw a part of a human flesh. And at that point, I started thinking of the worst. I didn't touch the area because I wanted to remember the good memories of my wife and my daughters. And at that point, I knew nothing of what had really happened. When we moved two blocks further away, we went to the house where the young boy escaped the massacre. I met him, and he explained to me in detail what had happened. He is an eye-witness to what happened, and you can ask him for the detail of that tragic event.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hoxha. I'm just going to go back to the house that you have circled, the white house, number 1. You said it was 21 people staying there overnight while you were staying in the house next to it or the vicinity of that marked with number 2. How many people stayed with you in this -- where you have circled around with number 2?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The house marked number 2, it was me, my son-in-law, and a cousin of him, Gani Hoxha, and Luli Vejsa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And another one, interpreters couldn't get his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Can you repeat the last name of the person you stayed there with?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Behar Haxhiavdija.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Amongst these 21 people staying in the house circled with number 1, were there any men among these people?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: There was a 50-, 55-year-old man, but he had mental problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: If we could please have up 65 ter number -- sorry. I would like to seek to tender this annotated picture into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P0082 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And then if we could have up 65 ter number 02230. And the last page of the English version, I believe it's page number 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, is this point in the transcript correct, it says P0082. Isn't it P00882, this picture?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: P00882. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to have this sketch over the whole screen, usher. It would be nice. Are you able to zoom it in a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you zoom in a little bit so that I can read better?

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: How is it now, Mr. Hoxha, are you able to read the names now, or would you like it to be zoomed in even further?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: If it's possible, let's zoom in a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, would you please explain to the Court what this sketch is, what is it showing?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: This sketch has been drafted in Tirana by me and another young man where I lived. This shows the names of all the victims except for my name here at the top, Hani Hoxha. This is my wife, Shahindere Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... would read out what you would like to describe?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Shahindere Hoxha, it's my wife. 56 years old. My late daughter Flaka Hoxha, born in 1983. This is my close family. So I have lost my wife and my daughter Flaka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Who made this list [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: This was drafted by me and a young man in Tirana who helped me do this. I told him the names, and he helped me design this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: There are in total 23 names on this list, and there are three names saying "alive" underneath?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Would you be able to list those three names that you explained on the sketch --

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: The people who were alive, it's Hani Hoxha, myself; Lulezim Vejsa, my son-in-law; and the son-in-law of my son-in-law, Behar Haxhiavdija. I do not see here the name of the one who escaped the massacre, but it seems it's not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: What would be the name of the person who escaped?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: I mentioned his name, it's Drini Caka.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: I think you are correct in that, it's not mentioned in the list. Is it then correct that the rest of the people on this list were present in this house and got killed under the attack?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: And would all of these 20 people -- were all of these 20 people women except from this 55-year-old man you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: No. The son of my daughter was there, five-year-old Arlind Vejsa. He is male. There is also a another boy, the son of Behar or somebody else, I can't remember. I think it's Behar's son. He was five year old too, a male. And the boy who is alive, who escaped, there was also Hysen Gashi the brother of Fetije Vejsa. The rest were all women.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hoxha. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness, and the sketch is already there in the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, shall I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have nearly 10 minutes, is that less than practical, would you prefer to commence again on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Friday, we are already tired and there are only seven or eight minutes left, but I can do the introductions. I think we'll deal with this witness very briefly and quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hani Hoxha. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a member of the Defence team for the accused Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic. And I'm assisted by Ms. Marie O'Leary, a member of our team. I have a few points to clear up with you, certain things you have said in your statement. I have read all your statements and all the transcripts of your testimony, and I'm familiar with your evidence. I will try to concentrate only on those things that nobody has asked you so far. To begin with, would I be right in saying that you are not an eye-witness to any of the events you testified to? I mean, the events and incidents you spoke about. You did not see any of them?

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: That's correct. I haven't seen the executions. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HANI HOXHA
utterances.text: But that does not mean that there are no eye-witnesses to that tragedy. And the eye-witnesses that I have spoken to, they are prepared to come and testify if they are required to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Hoxha. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the microphone working? It's on. Mr. Hoxha, I wish to express my very sincere condolences on behalf of my client and on behalf of our team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Nilsen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NILSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution do not have any further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hoxha, you will be pleased to know that because we are conscious that you need to be away, there is no need for any further questions of you. The Chamber has received your statement and the transcript of the evidence you've given twice now. I think once in the Milosevic trial, and once in the Milutinovic trial. And the Chamber will give some serious attention to that as we come to consider the evidence. And the Chamber has also the opportunity now to study at some length the very helpful chart that has been prepared, setting out the people of your family and others who were killed that night and which you've been able to set out very carefully for us. All of that has been of great assistance, and we are very thankful to you for what you've been able to do, and thankful to you that you've been prepared once again to come to The Hague to assist us. But given the circumstances, we are pleased to be able to say that you do not have a need to answer any more questions and that you are free to go back to your home or as you wish from now. We wish you well on your journey home, and we hope that you manage to continue to find a suitable way of having a satisfactory life. Thank you, sir, and you may now go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are very grateful for the tact shown in respect of the last witness. This seems an appropriate time now, of course, to conclude for the day. We resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday the 8th day of June 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
